blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Tree-species composition shapes forest productivity and how forests respond to climate disturbances such as drought, windthrow and insect outbreaks. Yet most national forest maps assign each pixel a single dominant species and cannot show the share of accompanying species. We mapped the basal-area shares of ten main tree species and a residual Other class across Switzerland at 30 m resolution. A deep-learning model combining 0.1 m aerial RGB imagery, airborne laser scanning (ALS), annual AlphaEarth satellite embeddings, and climate variables was trained on basal-area observations from 3,992 Swiss National Forest Inventory (NFI) sites. In spatial cross-validation, the model reached a macro-$R^2$ of 0.485 across the 11 classes. On an independent forest-reserve dataset, the map reached a macro-$R^2$ of 0.552 for individual 30 m pixels and 0.733 for plots, and identified the dominant class in 73.2% of pixels and 81.1% of plots. The map shows maple and ash as widespread minor components that dominant-class maps omit. It also reproduces the elevational sequence from broadleaved lowland stands through spruce to larch and Arolla pine near the treeline. By resolving the species mixture within each 30 m pixel, the map complements field inventory statistics with spatially continuous information that can support forest monitoring, the management of mixed stands, and climate-adaptation planning across Switzerland.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Accurate, spatially explicit information on tree-species composition is
essential for understanding how forests function and respond to
disturbances. Tree diversity is positively associated with forest
productivity ( Liang et al., 2016 ) , and species differ in their
susceptibility to drought, windthrow and insect outbreaks ( Anderegg et al., 2020 ; Senf and Seidl, 2021 ) . Forest services need
composition information to assess current forest condition and to select
species for climate-adapted regeneration ( Fassnacht et al., 2016 ; Strauss and Fischer, 2025 ) . In mixed forests, this
information goes beyond the dominant species. In other words, stands with the same dominant species can differ widely in the number and proportions of accompanying
species. Large-area composition maps therefore need to quantify the shares
of all species in a stand, including the accompanying ones ( Bolyn et al., 2022 ; Klehr et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.en:
Remote sensing (RS) has made large-area tree-species mapping increasingly
feasible by combining wall-to-wall image coverage with forest-inventory
observations. Satellite time series record seasonal differences among
species and provide repeated observations over large, environmentally
diverse regions ( Blickensdörfer et al., 2024 ; Breidenbach et al., 2021 ) .
Combined with national inventory data, they support products that
distinguish multiple species or species groups, including a 10 m map of
the dominant species in Switzerland ( Koch et al., 2024 ) . Most of these products,
however, assign a single class to each pixel. At resolutions of 10–30 m,
one pixel can cover several crowns and species, so a single class leaves
the within-pixel composition unresolved ( Fassnacht et al., 2016 ) . More
accurate classifiers make the dominant label more reliable, but they
still do not quantify the shares of secondary species.
Mixed stands also complicate the construction of reference data.
Restricting training samples to homogeneous or nearly pure stands
simplifies the link between image and label, but it underrepresents mixed
conditions during model development. Evaluating on pure stands alone then
gives an incomplete picture of performance where mixtures are common ( Blickensdörfer et al., 2024 ) .

each reference unit as a vector of species proportions. Such targets have
been learned from inventory data of mixed stands with spectral–spatial

Sentinel-2 time series ( Klehr et al., 2025 ) , from airborne laser

blocks.en:
Very-high-resolution aerial imagery provides evidence that freely available
satellite pixels cannot. At 0.1 m resolution, individual crowns, their texture and their
arrangement are visible, and such imagery has supported individual-tree
detection and species identification in Swiss forests ( Beloiu et al., 2023 ) . Switzerland acquires such imagery for its
entire territory on a roughly three-year cycle ( Federal Office of Topography
swisstopo, 2026b ) . Using it for composition mapping, however,
poses a different learning problem. Inventory plots record the species and
diameter of individual trees, but these records are not matched to crowns
in the image, so a model must relate the appearance of a whole canopy patch
to the plot-level composition. Self-supervised models pretrained on large
unlabeled image collections provide features that transfer to forest
imagery with few labels ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) . Such features have
supported canopy height mapping ( Brandt et al., 2026 ) , but they have not
yet been tested for estimating species composition from inventory plots.

blocks.en:
Other observations, such as satellite time series, airborne laser
scanning, and climate data, may add what a single aerial acquisition misses.
Species that look alike on one date can differ in their seasonal
trajectories ( Cloutier et al., 2024 ) , and annual satellite embeddings
summarize such trajectories from several sensors ( Brown et al., 2025 ; Ball et al., 2026 ) . Airborne laser scanning describes
canopy structure ( Murray et al., 2024 ) , and climate variables
describe where each species can grow ( Blickensdörfer et al., 2024 ) .
Combining these sources with aerial imagery is not straightforward. They
differ in spatial support, from 0.1 m image pixels to 10 m embeddings and
1 km climate grids, and in acquisition date. With few training plots, a
model may also rely on covariates that mainly encode location, such as
climate, instead of on what the imagery shows. Fusing satellite imagery and
lidar has improved composition estimates ( Candelas Bielza et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) , but most of this work
did not include very-high-resolution aerial imagery, so little is known
about what these sources add to it.

blocks.en: Here, we aim to develop a national, spatially continuous map of tree-species composition for Switzerland, representing the basal-area shares of 10 main tree species and an Other class rather than assigning each location to a single dominant species. We specifically ask: i) Within an RGB-anchored multimodal framework, what predictive information does each remote-sensing and environmental data source contribute to tree-species composition mapping? ii) How accurately does the national map estimate tree-species composition across independent spatial scales and datasets? iii) What ecological patterns of tree-species composition emerge across Switzerland’s elevational gradient? We hypothesize that integrating multimodal data enables accurate mapping of tree-species composition beyond inventory sites while preserving ecologically meaningful spatial patterns. We address these questions by combining basal-area observations from 3,992 Swiss National Forest Inventory sites with high-resolution aerial imagery, airborne laser scanning, satellite embeddings, and climate data in a multimodal deep-learning framework. We evaluate the contribution of the different data sources using spatial cross-validation, generate a 30 m national composition map, and independently evaluate it using Swiss Forest Reserves and regional NFI4 statistics. Continuous composition mapping provides a new basis for monitoring forest diversity and change.
blocks.zh: 在此,我们的目标是为瑞士绘制一个国家、空间连续的树种构成图,代表10个主要树种和1个其他类的玄武岩地区份额,而不是将每个地点分配给一个单一的主要物种。 我们特别问:一)在RGB-受控多模式框架内,每个遥感和环境数据来源对树种组成图谱的贡献是什么预测信息? (二) 国家地图如何准确估计独立空间尺度和数据集的树种组成? (三) 在瑞士的高地梯度中,树种构成的生态模式是什么? 我们假设,整合多模式数据有助于准确绘制库存地点以外的树种组成图,同时保持具有生态意义的空间格局。 我们通过将3 992个瑞士国家森林清单站点的玄武岩区域观测与高分辨率航空图像、空中激光扫描、卫星嵌入和气候数据结合到一个多模式的深入学习框架中来解决这些问题。 我们利用空间交叉验证评估不同数据来源的贡献,绘制出30米的国家构成图,并使用瑞士森林保护区和区域国家森林资料4统计数据进行独立评价。 持续的构成图绘制为监测森林多样性和变化提供了新的基础。

blocks.en:
Switzerland (41,285 km 2 ) spans pronounced elevational and climatic
gradients, from the low-lying Plateau and Jura foothills to the high Alps
(Fig. 1 a).
These gradients are important drivers of woody species distributions across
the country ( Wüest et al., 2020 ) . Forests cover 1.3 million hectares, or
32% of the land. Nationally, 61% of the forested area is coniferous and
39% broadleaved ( Strauss and Fischer, 2025 ) . Forest composition,
however, varies strongly among regions: coniferous, spruce-dominated stands
predominate in parts of the Alps, whereas broadleaved and
mixed forests occur more frequently at lower elevations and in the warmer
southern regions ( Strauss and Fischer, 2025 ; Wüest et al., 2020 ) .

blocks.zh: 2.2 参考标签构建

blocks.en:
The prediction taxonomy follows the Swiss NFI main-tree-species grouping ( Fischer and Traub, 2019 ; Strauss and Fischer, 2025 ) . Ten species or genera
are mapped separately: spruce, fir, pine, larch, Arolla pine, beech, maple,
ash, oak and chestnut. The remaining 48 retained taxa, both broadleaved and
coniferous, are pooled into an Other class (Table S3 ); example
sites of the ten species are shown in Fig. 5 b.
From 63,969 tree records at 5,998 NFI sites, we retained observations from
2017 onward, when SWISSIMAGE acquisitions become available for download ( Federal Office of Topography
swisstopo, 2026b ) . Upper- and middle-stratum trees were
retained, and understory trees were excluded because they are largely
hidden in nadir-viewing imagery. Canopy strata follow the NFI5 protocol ( Düggelin et al., 2020 ) . We also excluded sites affected by
stand-replacing disturbance between the field survey and RS acquisitions,
sites whose SWISSIMAGE imagery was degraded, mostly by terrain or cloud
shadow, and sites with incomplete multimodal records. The resulting dataset
contains 39,380 tree records at 3,992 sites surveyed in 2017–2022
(Fig. 1 b,c).

blocks.en: 2.3 Remote sensing and environmental data

blocks.en:
Four inputs were extracted around each NFI site coordinate: aerial RGB
imagery, airborne laser scanning (ALS) point clouds, annual satellite
embeddings, and climate variables (Table 2 ). Aerial imagery was obtained from
SWISSIMAGE, the 0.1 m RGB orthomosaic of the Swiss Federal Office of
Topography (swisstopo) ( Federal Office of Topography
swisstopo, 2026b ) . For each site, we
cropped a 28 m × \times 28 m square (280 × \times 280 pixels) centered on
the site coordinate. This extent slightly exceeds the 25.2 m diameter of the
outer NFI sample circle, so that the crop accommodates coordinate
uncertainty and crowns extending beyond the plot boundary. SWISSIMAGE is
renewed on a roughly three-year cycle, and acquisitions differ in season.
Leaf-on acquisitions were selected following Ferrari et al. (2027) .
Canopy structure was represented by swissSURFACE3D, the nationwide ALS
point cloud of swisstopo, with a mean density of about
15–20 points m -2 ( Federal Office of Topography
swisstopo, 2026c ) . Point clouds
were cropped to a 14 m-radius circle centered on each site and inscribed in
the RGB crop. Only the X X , Y Y , and Z Z coordinates and the point
classification were retained. Satellite information was represented by
annual, 64-dimensional AlphaEarth embeddings at 10 m resolution ( Brown et al., 2025 ) , from which a 3 × \times 3-pixel patch centered
on each site was extracted for the NFI survey year. Climate was
represented by the 19 CHELSA BIOCLIM+ variables for the 1981–2010
climatology at approximately 1 km resolution ( Brun et al., 2022 ) , read
at each site’s coordinate.

blocks.en: 3.1 Model architecture
blocks.zh: 3.1 示范架构

blocks.en:
Supervision is provided at the site level. Each training sample pairs the
30 m × \times 30 m footprint with its observed composition, so the model
learns to aggregate evidence over the whole footprint. The architecture has
three stages (Fig. 4 ). Modality-specific encoders
project each input into a shared D D -dimensional embedding space; a gated
fusion module combines these embeddings into a single site representation
anchored on the aerial imagery; and three heads predict the species
composition and two auxiliary targets, stand type and leaf type
(Section 3.1.3 ).

derived from the same basal-area observations. Stand type marks a site as
pure when its largest class share reaches 0.80 and as mixed otherwise.
Leaf type is the pair of broadleaved and coniferous shares of the expanded
basal area. It is computed from the original NFI taxa rather than from the
11 mapped classes, so the broadleaved and coniferous taxa within Other are
assigned to their own leaf type. Both
targets are easier to recognize than individual species and give the
shared representation additional supervision. The three targets are
predicted in parallel rather than hierarchically, so that an error in a
coarse target cannot propagate to the species predictions, as it can in
hierarchical classification ( Li et al., 2025 ; Ball et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Turkoglu et al., 2021 ) .
Three heads read 𝐡 \mathbf{h} : a linear layer for stand type, a linear
layer for leaf type, and a two-layer perceptron ( D → 256 → 11 D\to 256\to 11 ) for
composition, each followed by a softmax.

blocks.en: 3.2 Spatial cross-validation and training
blocks.zh: 3.2 空间交叉验证和培训

blocks.en:
To evaluate prediction at unseen locations while accounting for spatial
autocorrelation ( Roberts et al., 2017 ) , we grouped the 3,992
sites into 10 km spatial blocks and assigned entire blocks to five folds ( Abdi and Wang, 2026 ) . A greedy assignment balanced the fold sizes and the
mean basal-area share of each of the 11 classes across folds, a form of
spatially stratified block cross-validation ( Valavi et al., 2019 ) . The
folds were rotated through training and evaluation
(Fig. 5 a), and each site was predicted by the model
for which it was held out, so that all 3,992 sites enter the evaluation.
Each model was trained for 80 epochs with AdamW (learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.05, cosine decay to 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} ) and
a batch size of 4, with an exponential moving average of the weights
(decay 0.999). Sites containing rare classes were oversampled; further
settings are given in Supplementary Section S11 .

blocks.en: 3.3 National-scale mapping
blocks.zh: 3.3 国家规模测绘

blocks.en:
After model selection, the selected configuration was refitted on all 3,992
sites to obtain the production model. It was applied on a 30 m grid within
the forest mask of Ferrari et al. (2027) . The 30 m cell matches the
spatial support of the reference labels: at 99.0% of the sites, all
retained tree positions fall within a centered 30 m cell, compared with
65.5% for a 20 m cell. At each grid cell, we used the most recent leaf-on
SWISSIMAGE acquisition and the AlphaEarth embedding of the same year,
together with swissSURFACE3D and the CHELSA climatology. The reference year
of the map therefore varies between regions, from 2018 to 2025
(Fig. S3 ).

blocks.en: 3.4 Accuracy assessment
blocks.zh: 3.4 准确性评估

blocks.en:
Following Nelson et al. (2021) , we assessed the product from three
perspectives: site-specific accuracy, non-site-specific accuracy, and
spatial-distribution accuracy. For each class, we computed the mean
absolute error (MAE), the root mean squared error (RMSE), and the
coefficient of determination ( R 2 R^{2} ) between observed and predicted shares.
We averaged them over the classes (macro-average), so that every class
contributes equally regardless of its abundance. Each composition vector
was also converted to its dominant class, for which we report overall
accuracy and macro- F 1 F_{1} . Cross-validation metrics are reported as the
mean ± \pm standard deviation over the five held-out folds.

Site-specific accuracy was assessed with the cross-validated predictions at
the 3,992 NFI sites and with the forest reserve data
(Section 2.4 ) at two supports. At plot level, the
prediction was the intersection-area-weighted mean of all 30 m pixels
overlapping the plot polygon. At pixel level, we retained pixels at least
80% covered by a plot and containing at least 10 trees, and compared each
with its own prediction (414 pixels from 111 plots in 34 reserves).
Chestnut occurs in only one reserve plot, so its R 2 R^{2} cannot be
evaluated, and reserve R 2 R^{2} is averaged over the remaining ten classes. Non-site-specific accuracy was assessed against the published NFI4
basal-area shares of the five production regions ( Abegg et al., 2023 ) , for which the predicted shares were averaged
over the forest pixels of each region. Spatial-distribution accuracy was
assessed along the elevation gradient. Terrain elevation from swisstopo
swissALTIRegio ( Federal Office of Topography
swisstopo, 2026a ) , a 10 m model based on
swissALTI3D within Switzerland, was area-averaged onto the 30 m product
grid. Predicted shares were then averaged within 100 m elevation bands, and
only bands containing at least 5,000 forest pixels (4.5 km 2 ) were
analyzed.

blocks.en:
Continuous basal-area shares revealed widespread secondary species that
were largely absent from the dominant-class map
(Figs. 6 and 7 ). Maple and
ash, for example, rarely formed the dominant class but occurred as minor
components across extensive parts of the Swiss Plateau and Jura. By
contrast, larch, Arolla pine, and chestnut showed more spatially
concentrated distributions and reached high basal-area shares primarily
where they also formed the dominant class. The 30 m product covered
about 13,516 km 2 of Swiss forest. At reserve scale, the product
distinguished the fine-grained beech–spruce mosaic at Combe Biosse, the
fir–spruce mixture at Leihubelwald, and the nearly monospecific pine
stand at Pfynwald (Fig. 6 ).

blocks.en: 5 Discussion
blocks.zh: 5 讨论情况

blocks.en: 5.1 Value of continuous composition maps
blocks.zh: 5.1 联合国 连续构成图的价值

blocks.en:
Existing national products for Switzerland describe either the dominant
tree species ( Koch et al., 2024 ) or the leaf type ( Waser et al., 2017 ; Waser et al., 2025 ) . Our product adds the
basal-area share of each mapped class, from which a dominant-class map can
still be derived (Fig. 6 ). This difference matters
most for species that are common but rarely dominant. Maple and ash, for
example, occurred as minor components across much of the Plateau and Jura
but seldom formed the dominant class, so they are largely invisible in a
dominant-class map. These species contribute to the structural and
functional diversity of mixed stands, and their presence can influence how
a stand responds when its dominant species declines.
blocks.zh:
瑞士现有的国家产品说明两种主要产品是:
树种(Koch等,2024年)或叶类(Waser等,2017年;Waser等,2025年). 我们的产品增加了
每个绘图类的玄武岩面积份额,从中可得出占支配地位的类别地图
仍可导出(图6). 这种差别很重要
多数是常见但很少占支配地位的物种。 枫和灰,为
例如,在高原和汝拉的大部分地区作为小组成部分发生
但很少形成主导阶层,所以它们大多是隐形的
占支配地位的地图。 这些物种有助于结构上和上层结构的形成。
混合立体的功能多样性及其存在可如何影响
当它的主要物种衰落时,立方就应答。

blocks.en:
The product also complements the NFI. The inventory provides design-based
statistics for regions from a sample of plots, whereas the map provides
spatially continuous estimates for every 30 m forest cell. The close
agreement with NFI4 regional shares indicates that the map preserves
aggregate abundance. It can therefore be used where the NFI sample is too
sparse, for example to describe composition within individual forest
districts or along environmental gradients, and as auxiliary information
for model-assisted estimation.
blocks.zh:
该产品还补充了国家综合指数。 库存提供基于设计
从地块样本中获得的区域统计数据,而地图提供了
每30米森林细胞空间连续估计数。 结束
与NFI4区域股的协议表明,地图保存
总计丰度。 因此,在NFI样本也存在的地方可以使用.
例如,用于描述单个森林内部的构成的稀有森林
区域或沿环境梯度,作为辅助信息
用于模型辅助估算。

blocks.en:
For management, continuous shares allow mixed stands to be characterized
by their actual mixture rather than by a single label. In the montane
belt, spruce, beech, and fir co-occurred in comparable proportions
(Fig. 11 ), a situation that a dominant-class map reduces
to whichever species is marginally largest. Such information can help to
identify stands in which a vulnerable species dominates, or in which
admixed species already provide options for climate-adaptive silviculture.

对管理层来说,连续的股份允许对混合的票面进行定性
由它们的实际混合物而不是单一标签。 在蒙塔内
腰带、发芽、发芽和发纤维的混合含量相当
(图11),一个占支配地位的一等地图减少的情况
以最小的物种为准 此类信息有助于
确定一个脆弱物种占主导地位的位置,或
混合物种已经为适应气候的疏林提供了选择。

blocks.en: 5.2 Independent generalization and scale-dependent accuracy
blocks.zh: 5.2 独立概括和依规模而定的准确性

blocks.en:
The map generalized to the independent forest-reserve inventory, which
entered no stage of model development. At the native 30 m support, its
accuracy was comparable to, and in R 2 R^{2} slightly higher than, that of the
spatial cross-validation. Two differences between the reference datasets
may explain why the independent evaluation was not worse. The reserve
inventories record every tree within a plot polygon, whereas NFI labels are
derived from concentric sample circles in which trees below 36 cm DBH are
recorded on only 200 m 2 and weighted by expansion factors, so the NFI
labels carry more sampling noise. The reserve pixels also had to contain at
least 10 trees, which excludes the sparsest cells. Accuracy increased
further at plot support, consistent with the smoothing effect of averaging
predictions over several pixels. Validation results should therefore be
interpreted at the spatial support at which the product is used ( Ohmann et al., 2014 ; Koma and Breidenbach, 2025 ) : plot-level evidence for
aggregated applications, and the pixel-level or cross-validation estimates
for individual pixels.

blocks.en:
The comparison with NFI4 complements this site-specific evidence by showing
that the map also preserves regional species abundance. Similar agreement
between remotely sensed species maps and NFI-based regional proportions has
been reported elsewhere, with differences depending on inventory sample
size and the estimator ( Francini et al., 2024 ) . The remaining
disagreement was systematic: spruce was underestimated, Other was
overestimated, and the regression slope of 0.885 indicated moderate
compression toward intermediate shares. Part of this pattern may arise from
the estimands. NFI4 shares are ratios of regional mean basal-area densities
and are therefore weighted toward stands with a high basal area, whereas
map shares are unweighted means of pixel-level proportions.
Spruce-dominated stands often carry a high basal area, so this weighting
would raise the NFI4 share of spruce relative to the map. Heterogeneity
within Other and regression toward the mean may also contribute.

blocks.en: 5.3 Ecologically consistent elevational zonation
blocks.zh: 5.3 联合国 生态一致性高地分区

blocks.en:
The mapped forest area is unevenly distributed across the compositional
zones (Fig. 11 ): it peaks between 500 and 700 m, where the
product places beech-dominated stands, and declines steadily above
1,200 m. The elevational sequence the product recovers matches the
classical zonation of Central European mountain forests ( Ellenberg and Leuschner, 2010 ) , from oak-, chestnut-, and ash-rich lowland
stands through beech and fir to spruce, and finally to larch and Arolla
pine at the treeline. Between about 800 and 1,200 m, spruce, beech, and fir
each held 17–43% of the basal area, so this montane belt is where the
mixture information of a continuous product is most informative. The
conifer-dominated belt above roughly 1,200 m coincides with the elevations
at which nationwide standing deadwood peaks ( Ferrari et al., 2027 ) , so
a map of where those conifers stand is directly relevant to locating
forests exposed to drought-driven mortality. This agreement should be read
as a check on ecological plausibility rather than as independent evidence
of accuracy: the climate branch of the model carries information that is
itself strongly correlated with elevation.

blocks.en:
The RGB-only model reached R 2 = 0.452 R^{2}=0.452 , and the three

crown shape, texture, and local stand arrangement, consistent with Beloiu et al. (2023) , who distinguished major tree species in Swiss
forests from aerial RGB imagery. A larger image encoder improved accuracy
more than a different pretraining corpus, which suggests that encoder
capacity limits how much of this information is extracted.

blocks.en: 5.5 Limitations and future research
blocks.zh: 5.5 局限性和今后的研究

blocks.en:
The main limitation is that the structural information carried by ALS
was not fully exploited. The ALS encoder was trained from random
initialization on only 3,992 sites, and the swissSURFACE3D point clouds,
with a mean density of about 15–20 points m -2 , resolve fine vertical
canopy structure only coarsely ( Michałowska and Rapiński, 2021 ) . The first
nationwide campaign was also flown between 2017 and 2024, so the point
cloud and the aerial image of a site can be several years apart. These
factors may partly explain the confusion among spruce, fir, and Arolla
pine (Fig. 9 ), three dark-foliage conifers that
are difficult to separate by tone and texture in RGB imagery. Pretraining
the ALS encoder on unlabeled point clouds, or retraining it on the second
nationwide survey that swisstopo plans to complete by 2030 ( Federal Office of Topography
swisstopo, 2025 ) , may recover more of this
information.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusions
blocks.zh: 6. 结论

blocks.en:
We mapped the basal-area shares of ten main tree species and a residual
Other class across Switzerland at 30 m resolution by combining national
forest-inventory observations with multimodal remote sensing and climate
data. Aerial RGB imagery provided most of the predictive information,
with satellite embeddings and climate data providing additional gains.
Independent forest-reserve inventories and regional NFI4 statistics
supported the map’s ability to represent composition across spatial
scales, with higher accuracy when predictions were aggregated over plots.
The continuous shares captured both the broad elevational zonation of
Swiss forests and mixtures obscured by dominant-class maps, including
widespread accompanying species and the co-occurrence of spruce, beech,
and fir in the montane belt.

blocks.en:
The map shows that much of the compositional variation in Swiss forests
lies below the level of the dominant species. Maple and ash, for example,
rarely dominate a pixel. Yet they occur as minor components across large
parts of the Plateau and Jura. Such admixtures determine which species a
stand can fall back on if its dominant species declines under drought or
other disturbances. The map resolves the share of each main species at
30 m, making these admixtures visible at the national scale. Composition
can thus be located and compared across the country, extending beyond
regional inventory summaries. Repeated acquisitions could also allow
changes in composition to be followed through time.

blocks.en:
Approximately one-ninth of the permanent NFI plots are assessed each year
in annually rotating panels, allowing inventory statistics to be updated
continuously ( Fischer and Traub, 2019 ) .

blocks.en:
At each NFI sample point, field crews record trees within two concentric
circular plots defined by DBH (measured 1.3 m above ground): all trees and shrubs with DBH ≥ \geq 12 cm are recorded
within an inner 200 m 2 circle (7.98 m radius), and all trees and shrubs
with DBH ≥ \geq 36 cm are additionally recorded within an outer 500 m 2 circle (12.62 m radius) ( Fischer and Traub, 2019 ; Düggelin et al., 2020 ) . Species identity, DBH, canopy position, and
coordinates are recorded for every measured tree; canopy-layer assignment
follows relative height within the stand, stratified into an upper layer
(Oberschicht, ≥ \geq 2/3), a middle layer (Mittelschicht, 1/3–2/3), and an
understory (Unterschicht, ≤ \leq 1/3). The upper and middle strata are retained for the labels in
Section 2.2 .
A detailed description of the NFI sampling design is available in the
official inventory-concept documentation ( Swiss National Forest
Inventory, 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Rare-species representation was addressed by a distributed rare-site
weighted sampler. Pine, larch, Arolla pine, maple, ash, oak, and chestnut
were designated as rare classes. A site received a sampling weight of 1.5
if any of these classes reached a 5% basal-area share, regardless of which
class was dominant; all other sites received a weight of 1.0. Sampling was

than its contribution to the loss (Section 3.1.3 ). In the
single-GPU experiments, each epoch contained as many draws as there were
sites in the corresponding training fold, so individual sites could be
repeated or omitted within an epoch. Whenever a site was sampled again, its

Table S12 compares the per-class result of this
cross-validation with the pixel-level independent validation. Agreement
is not uniform across classes. Beech and larch have low MAE at both
supports, and larch also has similar R 2 R^{2} values, whereas beech’s R 2 R^{2} increases from 0.673 in cross-validation to 0.811 in the pixel-level
validation. Pine shows the clearest consistent deterioration: MAE, RMSE,
and dominant-class recovery (Section 4.3.1 ) are all worse
at the pixel level.
Several other classes show large R 2 R^{2} shifts driven by the reference
composition rather than by prediction error: maple’s MAE and RMSE are
both smaller at the pixel level (0.025 and 0.062, against 0.051 and
0.124 in the cross-validation) yet its R 2 R^{2} falls from 0.258 to 0.021,
because the standard deviation of the pixel-level reference share is
much smaller than that of the cross-validation sites. This is the same
mechanism documented for chestnut above: R 2 R^{2} is one minus a residual
sum of squares divided by the observed variance (Eq. S5 ), so a
smaller observed variance can lower R 2 R^{2} even when the absolute error
improves.
